quiz_item.question: Your patrol is hiking across an open alpine ridgeline when towering cumulonimbus clouds build rapidly and you hear thunder 10 seconds after seeing a lightning flash (roughly 2 miles away). What is the safest immediate action for the patrol?
options: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
choices: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Sound travels about 1 mile every 5 seconds; a 10-second flash-to-bang interval means lightning is within 2 miles and already in strike range, requiring immediate descent from ridges and avoidance of tall isolated objects.

pamphlet_excerpts: Routine Air Mass Changes: People readily adapt to routine weather changes that occur with the passage of air masses (p. 29).
Violent and Extreme Weather: Sometimes, however, the weather can become so violent or the temperature so extreme that people need to take special precautions (p. 29).
National Weather Service Alerts: Forecasters with the National Weather Service issue watches, warnings, and advisories to alert the public to potentially violent or hazardous (p. 29).
Watch Versus Warning Distinction: There is an important difference between a watch and a warning (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Monitor Official Weather Alerts: Forecasters with the National Weather Service issue watches, warnings, and advisories to alert the public to potentially violent or hazardous (p. 29).
Step 2 - Distinguish Alert Levels: There is an important difference between a watch and a warning (p. 29).
Step 3 - Prepare During Weather Watches: A watch means that hazardous weather is possible or that conditions are favorable for it to develop (p. 29).
Step 4 - Seek Shelter Under Warnings: A warning is a more urgent notice that hazardous conditions already exist or are heading your way (p. 29).

pamphlet_excerpts: First Weather Satellite Launch: The first weather satellite, known as TIROS-1, was launched in the spring of 1960 (p. 33).
Viewing Complete Storm Systems: It was highly successful at giving meteorologists their first overall view of entire storm systems (p. 33).
Continuous Global Storm Monitoring: Since then, satellites have become much more sophisticated, allowing a nearly continuous watch over the entire Earth (p. 33).
Primary Weather Satellite Types: Polar-orbiting satellites and geostationary satellites (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Track Global Satellite Imagery: Since then, satellites have become much more sophisticated, allowing a nearly continuous watch over the entire Earth (p. 33).
Step 2 - Compare Satellite Orbit Types: Polar-orbiting satellites and geostationary satellites (p. 33).
Step 3 - Use POES and GOES: The satellite systems are named Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES) and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (p. 33).
Step 4 - Analyze Polar Orbit Data: The polar-orbiting satellites circle Earth, passing over or near the poles at a height of approximately 520 miles (p. 33).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Your patrol is hiking across an open alpine ridgeline when towering cumulonimbus clouds build rapidly and you hear thunder 10 seconds after seeing a lightning flash (roughly 2 miles away). What is the safest immediate action for the patrol?
options: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
choices: A. Stay on the ridgeline under a tall isolated pine tree to keep dry until the rain passes.

B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
C. Huddle together in a tight circle on top of metal-frame backpacks.
D. Lie flat on wet granite at the summit so the wind blows over the patrol.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule: immediately descend off the exposed ridge and away from tall isolated trees or water, move into lower dense timber or a substantial building, and spread patrol members at least 50 feet apart if caught in the open.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Sound travels about 1 mile every 5 seconds; a 10-second flash-to-bang interval means lightning is within 2 miles and already in strike range, requiring immediate descent from ridges and avoidance of tall isolated objects.

C. Local Doppler weather radar towers

choices: A. Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES)

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What happens when an advancing cold front meets a mass of warmer air?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What happens when an advancing cold front meets a mass of warmer air?
options: A. Cold air rises high above the warm air mass and dissipates all clouds
B. Warm and cold air mix evenly without vertical motion or precipitation
C. Cold air glides gently on top of the warm air across hundreds of miles
D. Dense cold air stays near the surface and wedges beneath the warm air, forcing it upward
choices: A. Cold air rises high above the warm air mass and dissipates all clouds
B. Warm and cold air mix evenly without vertical motion or precipitation
C. Cold air glides gently on top of the warm air across hundreds of miles
D. Dense cold air stays near the surface and wedges beneath the warm air, forcing it upward
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Dense cold air stays near the surface and wedges beneath the warm air, forcing it upward
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Because cold air is denser than warm air, it stays near the surface and wedges beneath the warmer air, forcing the warm air to rise rapidly along a steep slope (p. 29).

options: A. It burns away excess oxygen in the upper stratosphere
B. It converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form that plants can absorb as fertilizer
C. It melts high-altitude cirrus clouds into warm summer rain
D. It neutralizes barometric pressure differences across the equator
choices: A. It burns away excess oxygen in the upper stratosphere
B. It converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form that plants can absorb as fertilizer
C. It melts high-altitude cirrus clouds into warm summer rain
D. It neutralizes barometric pressure differences across the equator
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form that plants can absorb as fertilizer
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Lightning converts nitrogen in the air into compounds that dissolve in rain and can be absorbed by plants as natural fertilizer (p. 34).
